item.title: A new fellowship is all about putting the news in news creator
item.description: The Columbia Journalism School is launching the News Creator Fellowship, a year-long program designed to support independent journalists and content creators producing original news outside traditional media. The fellowship will provide a $75,000 stipend, access to university resources, mentorship, workshops, workspace, and collaboration opportunities. The program aims to support individuals from diverse backgrounds producing news content on various platforms and who demonstrate a commitment to public service and pushing the boundaries of news. Applications for the inaugural cohort, starting in September 2026, are open now.

item.title: News Consumers are Content Creators in an AI-Driven World
item.description: The lines between news consumers and content creators are fading because of artificial intelligence. This shift began with the rise of the internet, social media, and smartphones, leading to participatory journalism and citizen reporting. AI tools now amplify this trend, providing automated content generation, media editing, and personalized curation, along with potential for fact-checking. Consumers are also curators and gatekeepers, influencing the visibility of information through their interactions. This new reality brings responsibilities, including combating misinformation, understanding AI's role, and promoting media literacy. The future of news involves active consumer participation, offering opportunities for a diverse information landscape alongside challenges in maintaining accuracy.

item.title: News Consumers and Content Creators
item.description: The article discusses the evolving relationship between news consumers and news creators, highlighting how digital technologies have lowered barriers to news creation. This shift presents both challenges and opportunities for professional news organizations. Challenges include potential loss of control over narratives, quality control issues with user-generated content, and financial strains. Opportunities include expanded coverage, diverse perspectives, and increased audience engagement. To navigate this landscape, the article suggests strategies like curating and verifying user-generated content, forming partnerships, providing media literacy education, and integrating technology. The piece concludes that a collaborative, innovative, and education-focused approach is crucial for building more inclusive and democratic information ecosystems.

item.title: News Consumers are Content Creators
item.description: In today's interconnected world, the roles of news consumers and content creators are merging. Individuals are no longer just absorbing information; they are actively participating in its distribution and interpretation. This shift is creating a new media landscape, exemplified by the rise of the "prosumer." Consumers become creators through sharing, commenting, citizen journalism, fact-checking, and user-generated content. This trend offers opportunities for democratization, increased engagement, and faster information dissemination, especially for local and niche content. However, it also presents challenges like the spread of misinformation, echo chambers, quality control issues, and privacy concerns. News organizations and individuals alike are adapting to these evolving responsibilities, recognizing the impact of participatory news consumption on shaping narratives and public opinion. This evolving process of news consumption brings challenges regarding accuracy and bias, while simultaneously providing unprecedented opportunities for democratization, engagement, and the amplification of diverse voices, which is essential to understanding the modern information landscape.

item.title: Some more personal news: October 2025
item.description: Jay Rosen is announcing his retirement from NYU, effective January 1, 2026. His final day of teaching will be December 18, 2025, and his last day on salary will be December 31, 2025. He will continue as Professor Emeritus of Journalism and plans to maintain Pressthink. He expresses gratitude to NYU and his students and readers. He also mentions he will be teaching two courses in the Fall of 2025 and provides enrollment details for interested NYU students.

item.title: Some more personal news
item.description: After retiring from NYU's Journalism department, the author is taking on a part-time Senior Fellow position at the Lenfest Institute for Journalism. This role will involve advising, writing, and public appearances, drawing on the author's expertise regarding the evolving role of the press and the challenges facing local news. The Lenfest Institute is a funder of local news organizations and the author has a history with the institute, having previously served on its board.

item.title: Some More Personal News, October 2025
item.description: In October 2025, it was announced that the author, after five years at New York University, would be leaving their position as Professor of Journalism and Silly Walks and Director of the Studio 20 Program. Their last day at NYU will be December 31, 2025. They will be joining the University of California, Berkeley, as Professor of Digital Media and Silly Walks at the Graduate School of Journalism and Director of the New Media Innovation Studio, beginning January 1, 2026. The move was a difficult decision, but the opportunity at Berkeley and the chance to work with Professor Python were major draws. They and their family will be moving to Berkeley in late December.

item.title: Denialism as an Area of Study
item.description: A 4-post Bluesky thread by Jay Rosen. Thread depth: 3 levels.

item.title: Jay Rosen (@jayrosen_nyu): This is not some one-off gaffe. It's an entire system of illusion that runs on bad faith and manufactured ignorance.
item.description: The author suggests a key indicator of an "informational hellscape" is when journalists believe their duty is to present both sides of an issue fairly, even when one side is deliberately spreading falsehoods and the other is presenting accurate information, while also questioning what alternatives the journalists have.

item.title: ABC goes too far in pushing out Terry Moran; plus, Google’s AI assault, and Jay Rosen moves on
item.description: This episode of the podcast 'Drilled' discusses the impact of Big Oil's propaganda machine and explores potential solutions to the current disinformation crisis. NYU journalism professor Jay Rosen and former FCC commissioner Nicholas Johnson discuss various approaches, from the Fairness Doctrine and cable access to navigating the 'post-fact' world.

item.title: Some personal news
item.description: Jay Rosen reflects on his 39-year career as an NYU journalism professor, highlighting his work on the concept of a public service press, his engagement with the rise of digital media and blogging, and his contributions to journalism education. He emphasizes the importance of seeing people as a public, critiquing detached journalism and advocating for increased audience participation. Rosen's work, from his book 'What Are Journalists For?' to his blog PressThink and collaborations like 'Off the Bus', aimed to bridge the gap between journalists and their audiences.

item.title: Reflections on 39 Years at NYU: A Retirement Thread

item.title: Trump, Truth, and 'Freedom from Fact': Jay Rosen with Adrian Goldberg at the Byline Festival
item.description: Jay Rosen discusses the potential implications of a Trump election in 2024, focusing on Trump's freedom from fact approach to politics and the changing media landscape. He highlights the Republican Party's support for Trump, the dangers of Project 2025, and Trump's manipulation of the media to create chaos and undermine established facts, as well as the fragmentation of the media world and the isolation of Trump's supporters from mainstream news sources.

item.title: "When in Doubt, Draw a Distinction": Key Concepts in My Work
item.description: A 26-post Bluesky thread by Jay Rosen. Thread depth: 25 levels.

item.title: How Do You Report the News in a Post-Truth World?
item.description: The decline in trust in journalism, coupled with the rise of unreliable information sources like social media influencers and partisan platforms, is contributing to a post-truth environment. This crisis is impacting public understanding of critical issues such as climate change and election integrity. The article highlights Jay Rosen's perspective on the shared responsibility of journalists in this situation, suggesting that the profession itself needs critical examination and reform.

item.title: Jay Rosen and Taylor Owen: Can journalism survive Trump? Can democracy?
item.description: This podcast discussion between Jay Rosen and Taylor Owen explores the decline of trust in journalism and the challenges facing the profession in the face of political polarization and the rise of misinformation. They discuss the shift from traditional journalism's 'view from nowhere' to a more subjective approach, the impact of 'savvy journalism' focusing on political gamesmanship, and the phenomenon of 'verification in reverse' used by figures like Donald Trump to undermine established facts. The conversation highlights the need for a new approach to journalism that prioritizes transparency, accountability, and a commitment to democracy while acknowledging the inherent limitations and evolving nature of the media landscape.

item.title: Thinking about the people formerly known as the audience
item.description: The concept of the audience has evolved due to the internet, transforming passive recipients of news into active participants. The author reflects on this shift, highlighting how individuals now contribute to the conversation through comments, social media, and sharing information. While acknowledging the challenges of managing online engagement, such as dealing with negativity and misinformation, the core idea remains: the traditional passive audience is obsolete. News organizations and journalists must adapt by engaging with and involving individuals in the ongoing journalistic process, recognizing them as potential interlocutors.

item.title: Thinking about the "People Formerly Known As The Audience"
item.description: The author reflects on the phrase "the people formerly known as the audience," arguing it's become inaccurate. While acknowledging the shift from passive consumers to active participants, the author believes the audience still exists, albeit in a more demanding, interactive, and multifaceted form. They suggest reframing the public as the audience plus, recognizing their roles as creators, distributors, curators, and critics. This shift in perspective is crucial for developing effective media strategies, encouraging agencies to acknowledge audience agency, facilitate participation, understand their diverse roles, and value their feedback to effectively serve them in their redefined, more complex form.

item.title: The Media Can Build Back Trust by How It Covers Trump
item.description: Jay Rosen reflects on a quote by Raymond Williams, arguing that the concept of "the public" is not inherent but rather a constructed understanding of people as a collective. He posits that a failure to actively see people as a public will lead to declining support for public service journalism.

item.title: Inclusive journalism and the 2024 US elections: Tracking the coverage
item.description: This essay, published in TIME shortly before the 2024 election, urges political reporters to shift their focus from speculative worst-case scenarios and the “horse race” aspects of campaign coverage to a focus on the factual consequences of candidates' actions and policies. The author argues that excessive attention to threats and promises, rather than verifiable facts and their impact, fuels cynicism, breeds anticipatory obedience, and ultimately aids those in power. The author advocates for a reporting approach that prioritizes verifiable effects of policies over speculation and premonition, urging journalists to hold power accountable for what is actually done rather than what is said.

item.title: A Second Academic Exodus From X?
item.description: Stephen Colbert, on The Colbert Report, criticized NYU journalism professor Jay Rosen for his critique of Sunday morning talk shows' lack of fact-checking. Colbert disagreed with Rosen's suggestion that guests should be fact-checked, labeling Rosen "Field Marshall Thesaurus."

item.title: Jeff Bezos’ view from nowhere
item.description: The article critiques Jeff Bezos's view that the Washington Post should avoid endorsing political candidates to maintain credibility. It argues that this "view from nowhere" is outdated and trust-destroying in the modern media landscape where audiences expect transparency and authenticity. The author contends that building trust requires sharing perspectives and biases upfront, rather than pretending to be neutral.

item.title: Reporters speak at Deerfield Academy on the landscape of political journalism
item.description: A panel featuring Wall Street Journal's Annie Linskey, Politico's Meridith McGraw, and NYU professor Jay Rosen discussed the role of the press in shaping American elections at Deerfield Academy. The conversation covered journalistic bias, the pursuit of truth amidst misinformation, and the evolving dynamics of information flow. Panelists addressed concerns about echo chambers and the increasing tendency of audiences to seek information that confirms pre-existing beliefs, as well as the impact of AI and deepfakes on political journalism.

item.title: Jay Rosen (@jayrosen_nyu): The "real work of journalism" began after the initial news broke.
item.description: Jay Rosen's tweet provides an example of his commentary on journalism or media. It likely addresses a crucial issue, such as press coverage of an event or the changing role of the press in the digital age. He frequently offers perspectives on transparency, accountability, and the public's view of news organizations. The tweet garnered a moderate amount of engagement, including replies, reposts, likes, and views.

item.title: Thinking about “the people formerly known as the audience”
item.description: The author reflects on the phrase "the people formerly known as the audience," coined by Jay Rosen, highlighting the internet's impact on transforming media consumers into active participants. Legacy news organizations, like the New York Times, often struggle to adapt, still viewing readers as a passive audience rather than partners in newsgathering. The author suggests news organizations shift from being the sole arbiters of truth to facilitators, fostering collaborative conversations and valuing reader contributions. This involves changing mindsets, practices, and organizational culture, emphasizing transparency, participation, and a willingness to evolve to build trust and ensure the future of news.

item.title: Jay Rosen in Oz: On Horserace Journalism and the 2024 Election
item.description: So-called “horse-race” reporting—sound bite-driven, he-said-she-said, stat-obsessed, poll-heavy, strategy-focused—is a major draw whichever end of the equator you’re on. Rosen, scathing as ever about the state of modern electoral coverage, has been on TV, behind podiums, and in meeting rooms discussing “horse-race journalism,” which he defined in an interview on the Australian Broadcasting Corporation’s (ABC) Lateline as “a reusable model for how to do campaign coverage in which you focus on who’s going to win rather than what the country needs to settle by electing a prime minister.” “But the biggest advantage of horse-race journalism is that it permits reporters and pundits to ‘play up their detachment,’” Rosen has written.

item.description: This text is a collection of links and descriptions of Jay Rosen's work and online resources related to journalism, the internet, and the changing media landscape. It includes mentions of his book, "What Are Journalists For?", and various interviews, presentations, and blog recommendations. The excerpt also analyzes two contrasting perspectives on political publicity, one critical and the other admiring, highlighting the lack of a mature vocabulary to discuss publicity-driven events.

item.title: Media Critics Agree: Stop Interviewing the Bad People!
item.description: The article discusses the debate within the media regarding whether to interview Donald Trump. Critics argue that interviewing him legitimizes his actions and spreads misinformation, while others contend that avoiding him deprives the public of crucial information and strengthens his position. The author ultimately argues against deplatforming Trump, emphasizing the importance of journalistic perseverance and the potential for impactful reporting even when dealing with difficult figures.

item.title: A desperate appeal to newsroom leaders on the eve of a chaos election
item.description: Following Elon Musk's acquisition of Twitter (now X), a second wave of academics are leaving the platform, citing concerns about disinformation, toxicity, and Musk's support for Donald Trump. While some argue that academics should remain on X to reach a broader audience, others are migrating to platforms like Bluesky, highlighting a potential decline in the use of X by academics and a shift in how they engage with the public.

item.title: How 'verification in reverse' powers the conservative media bubble and right-wing politics
item.description: Jay Rosen discusses the concept of "verification in reverse," where established truths are questioned and denied to create energy and power for political movements, particularly within the conservative media landscape. He argues this approach, exemplified by figures like Trump and events like "Stop the Steal," fuels political asymmetry and challenges the traditional understanding of shared facts between parties. Rosen acknowledges the uncertain future of this dynamic, questioning whether it will lead to a crash or continue to shape American politics.

item.title: NYU journalism professor Jay Rosen: Fox is "the commercial wing of the MAGA movement that has overtaken the Republican party" | Media Matters for America
item.description: Jay Rosen, in an interview on MSNBC, argues that Fox News is not a news organization but rather the commercial wing of the MAGA movement, producing "resentment news." He explains that the Dominion court documents reveal how Fox News's power to manipulate its audience through resentment backfired when some Fox employees reported truthfully, causing an internal crisis. This crisis, Rosen contends, demonstrates that Fox News prioritizes its political agenda over journalistic integrity.

item.title: Thinking About the “People Formerly Known as the Audience”
item.description: The piece discusses the evolution of the public's relationship with information, drawing from Jay Rosen's concept of the "people formerly known as the audience." The internet and social media have transformed the public from passive consumers to active participants in the news cycle, influencing power dynamics. Politicians like Donald Trump have leveraged this shift by directly engaging with their supporters, bypassing traditional media. This democratization offers increased participation but also fosters misinformation and polarization as the lines between fact and opinion blur. The challenge lies in navigating this new landscape responsibly to promote productive dialogue and a shared sense of truth in an environment where everyone has the potential to be a content creator.

item.title: Why aren’t mainstream journalists sounding the alarm about the threat to democracy?
item.description: The article explores why mainstream political journalists aren't aggressively addressing the threat to democracy. It posits several theories, including the possibility that journalists are not truly alarmed by the threat or are unable to grasp its significance due to a lack of understanding of democracy's fragility, a lack of diversity in newsrooms, and a reliance on outdated journalistic norms of 'balance' that fail to adequately address a fundamentally asymmetric threat. The author highlights a Twitter discussion with prominent journalists and academics who agree that the issue is less about capability and more about will, perspective, and the profession's outdated practices.

item.title: Beyond the ‘Democracy Desk’: Why U.S. newsrooms need to become explicitly pro-democracy
item.description: The U.S. is experiencing democratic backsliding, weakening the informal systems that underpin democracy. The American press needs to become more explicitly pro-democracy, rather than treating it as an assumed background condition. This requires experimentation and a willingness to show what's at stake in the battle for American democracy, despite concerns about being perceived as partisan.

item.title: He used to edit political stories at the Chicago Tribune. Now he says the press is failing our democracy. - PressThink
item.description: This article is an interview with Mark Jacob, a retired journalist, who reflects on his experience in political journalism and critiques the "he said/she said" approach to news reporting. Jacob argues that this approach, prioritizing equal representation of both sides regardless of truthfulness, has been exploited by propagandists and has ultimately failed to serve democracy. He details how this approach, while intended to appear fair and objective, unintentionally enabled the spread of misinformation and undermined the power of fact-checking. He also discusses the various motivations behind this flawed approach, including commercial pressures, the pursuit of attention, and the fear of upsetting powerful figures or the public.

item.title: Andrew Tyndall comments on CBS News hiring Trump’s former chief of staff Mick Mulvaney as a news analyst and paid contributor
item.description: Andrew Tyndall analyzes the controversy surrounding CBS News's hiring of Mick Mulvaney, Donald Trump's former chief of staff, as a paid contributor. The analysis includes excerpts from a broadcast discussing the hiring, which was quickly reversed after internal criticism. The main reasons for the controversy were the impression that CBS was actively recruiting former Trump officials and Mulvaney's strong opinions on current national security issues. The author also notes that the hiring gave the impression of a move to bring more conservative voices to the network.

item.title: Answers to Craig's Questions - PressThink
item.description: This article presents a conversation between the author and Craig Newmark about lessons learned from the 2016 election regarding the trustworthiness of the press. Key takeaways include the press's flawed predictions, disconnect from large portions of the country, vulnerability to demagoguery, and challenges in dealing with disinformation and the erosion of truth in the Trump era. The conversation highlights shifts in journalistic practices, such as explicitly calling out lies and acknowledging the right-wing media's role in shaping reality, but also acknowledges ongoing challenges like the inability to effectively counter open corruption.

item.title: The savvy turn in political journalism - PressThink
item.description: This article examines the "savvy style" in American journalism, a tendency to prioritize political strategy and insider knowledge over factual accuracy and accountability. The author contrasts this approach with a "citizens agenda" model, exemplified by the Charlotte Observer's efforts to focus on voters' concerns. He argues that the savvy style, which accepts political maneuvering as a given, often prevents journalists from probing the justifications for actions and policies, as illustrated by the lack of scrutiny given to Republican opposition to voting rights legislation. The author concludes that the savvy temptation remains strong in American journalism, hindering effective public engagement.

item.title: After six years of asking, NPR interviewed Trump. A journalist for VICE asked me how it went.
item.description: Donald Trump was interviewed by NPR's Steve Inskeep, marking the first time in six years, and after Trump directly contacted Inskeep. The author, listening to the interview, found it interesting, commending Inskeep's handling of questions, including Trump's continued false claims about the 2020 election. A journalist from VICE then contacted the author for their thoughts on the interview, and the author conveyed their positive assessment, emphasizing the importance of NPR securing the interview despite Trump's false statements. The discussion also touched on the complexities of real-time fact-checking during interviews. Overall, the author considered the interview significant and valuable for hearing from different perspectives and challenging those in positions of power.

item.title: Professor Jay Rosen on 'pro-democracy' agenda for media
item.description: Jay Rosen discusses the challenges facing political journalism in an era where one of the two major political parties is exhibiting anti-democratic tendencies. He argues that traditional journalistic practices are inadequate when dealing with a party that rejects common facts and undermines democratic norms. Rosen suggests that news organizations should explicitly state their commitment to democracy, truth, science, evidence, and voting, and then revise their practices accordingly. He also advocates for a 'citizens' agenda' approach, focusing on voter priorities and using an 'urgency index' to assess the state of democratic backsliding.

item.title: The Possible End Of American Democracy As We Know It
item.description: Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist Barton Gellman argues in his new Atlantic article, "Trump's Next Coup Has Already Begun," that the Republican party is increasingly unwilling to accept defeat and is "prepared to win by sacrificing the essential elements of democracy." The text also mentions a review of Adele's album, 30, by Ken Tucker.

item.title: Transcript: Nicole Hemmer Interviews Jay Rosen for ‘The Ezra Klein Show’ - The New York Times
item.description: This transcript of an interview on "The Ezra Klein Show" features Jay Rosen discussing the shortcomings of mainstream media coverage, particularly concerning complex legislation like the Build Back Better bill. Rosen critiques the focus on incremental updates and "inside game" reporting, arguing that this prioritizes daily content production over genuine public understanding. He highlights the lack of an "architecture of understanding" in news coverage, leading to an overemphasis on strategy, speculation, and drama, rather than informing the public. The interview also touches upon the problematic use of terms like "moderate" and "centrist" in political journalism, and the challenges faced by the news industry in the digital age.

item.title: The "here's where we're coming from" statement in journalism - PressThink
item.description: The article discusses the shift from the traditional "view from nowhere" objectivity in journalism to a transparency-based approach where journalists disclose their perspectives and biases. It highlights examples like Casey Newton's newsletter Platformer and ProPublica, emphasizing the importance of journalists being upfront about their values and intentions to build trust with their audience. The piece also stresses the need for news organizations to adopt a broader transparency system, including disclosing ownership, funding, and decision-making processes.

item.title: A current list of my top problems in pressthink, May 2021 - PressThink
item.description: The article discusses the challenges faced by journalism in the current political climate, particularly with the rise of an anti-democratic Republican party that relies on counter-majoritarian and counter-factual narratives. It examines the inadequacy of the 'both sides' model of news coverage and the difficulty of determining newsworthiness in an era of disinformation. The author grapples with the dilemma of platforming harmful viewpoints while also needing to inform the public.

item.title: If you're worried that journalists have learned nothing from the Trump years.
item.description: This article discusses encouraging developments suggesting some journalists understand the need for change after the Trump presidency, the Stop the Steal movement, and the January 6th insurrection. It highlights examples such as WITF's policy of contextualizing future actions of officials who spread election fraud lies, the Cleveland Plain Dealer's refusal to amplify baseless claims, and ProPublica's creation of a democracy beat and Votebeat's efforts to build capacity within the American press to cover voting restrictions.

item.title: Prof. Jay Rosen was a guest on On The Media this week in a segment titled, "What The Press Have And Should Have Learned From The Trump Era." Also included in the same discussion was Yamiche Alcindor, NYU alum and White House correspondent for PBS NewsHour. - NYU Journalism
item.description: Jay Rosen discusses with Brooke Gladstone and Bob Garfield how the press has learned it is a subject in the story, especially during the Trump era, and argues that it must prioritize democracy over objectivity. He notes the emergence of a 'democracy beat' but criticizes the persistence of 'both-sidesism.' Rosen suggests the press should be more transparent and serve as a 'cheerleader' for the democratic process itself, holding power accountable for its commitment to democratic norms and values.

item.title: Two paths forward for the American press
item.description: The article discusses the future of the American press after Donald Trump's presidency. It contrasts two potential paths: a restoration of order and a return to normalcy, or a democratic breakthrough in journalism. The author critiques the media's longing for symmetry and 'both sides' narratives, even when facts don't warrant it, and highlights the importance of defending democracy and truth, as demonstrated by some journalists during the 2020 election.

item.title: America’s Press and the Asymmetric War for Truth
item.description: The Republican Party is increasingly becoming a minority party that relies on counterfactual narratives to maintain power. This creates a structural conflict with honest journalism, as the GOP must fight with fictions to appeal to its dwindling base. The Democratic Party is evolving into a coalition representing 'literally everyone else'.

item.title: America’s Press and the Asymmetric War for Truth
item.description: This article argues that the Republican Party's increasingly counter-majoritarian stance necessitates a conflict with honest journalism. The GOP's reliance on fictions, such as widespread voter fraud, clashes with reality-based reporting. The author criticizes mainstream media's tendency towards "he said/she said" journalism and "balanced treatment of unbalanced phenomena," arguing that this refuge-seeking behavior protects journalists from criticism rather than serving the public. He contends that the right-wing's creation of its own media ecosystem has shifted the dynamics, rendering traditional journalistic practices insufficient to address the asymmetrical political landscape.

item.title: Trump exploited a broken press. Here’s how to fix it.
item.description: The article discusses how Trump and his allies use the strategy of "flooding the zone with shit" to overwhelm the media and public with falsehoods, making it difficult for journalists to effectively counter the misinformation. Jay Rosen argues that the traditional journalistic code is inadequate to deal with this strategy, and the press needs to adapt by abandoning the "savvy style" and owning their agenda to effectively combat disinformation and protect democratic values.

item.title: You might not like it, but it's smart politics.
item.description: The article discusses how the press, particularly the political press corps, became overly focused on "savviness" and understanding politics as a strategic game played by insiders. This focus made them ill-equipped to cover the rise of Donald Trump and the challenges he posed to American democracy. The author argues for a shift in political journalism, emphasizing the defense of democracy, symmetrical accounts of asymmetrical realities, and a rejection of the "politics as strategic game" frame.

item.title: The Membership Guide: Handbook
item.description: This article defines membership in journalism as a social contract between a news organization and its members. It emphasizes the importance of memberful routines, a membership strategy, and a membership program. It distinguishes membership from subscription, donation, and crowdfunding models, highlighting the unique value proposition and expectations associated with each. The article draws on research from diverse member-driven movements to offer insights into successful membership programs, including the importance of listening to members, connecting to a larger purpose, offering flexible participation, and growing at a human scale.

item.title: Prof. Jay Rosen’s ideas were featured in Brian Stelter’s opening monologue on CNN’s media criticism program, Reliable Sources
item.description: Jay Rosen discusses the media's coverage of the jobs crisis, arguing that it's being treated as a political story rather than a national crisis. He suggests that the press is too focused on objectivity, the horse race in Washington, and is disconnected from the public's experience of unemployment. Rosen advocates for more stories about the real-life impact of unemployment and a shift towards public journalism that helps citizens solve problems.

item.title: Jay Rosen Presents “The Citizens Agenda”
item.description: Jay Rosen, a journalism professor, presented the idea of a "Citizens Agenda" to improve how journalists and news organizations serve the public. He suggests that instead of prioritizing politicians and political strategy, news outlets should identify and report on the issues that the public deems most important.

item.title: What I learned by watching the American press try to cover Donald Trump
item.description: Jay Rosen reflects on his observations of the American press's coverage of Donald Trump's presidency. He argues that the press's practices rest on assumptions about presidential behavior that don't apply to Trump, leading to a normalization of his actions rather than a critical examination. He introduces the concept of 'verification in reverse,' where publicly doubted claims are used to generate controversy and power political movements. He also notes the effectiveness of strategies like 'flooding the zone' (or the Russian equivalent, 'firehose of falsehoods') in undermining trust in journalism by overwhelming the truth with misinformation.

item.title: NYU Professor Jay Rosen Tears Chuck Todd Over Trump Lies
item.description: Jay Rosen critiques Chuck Todd's Rolling Stone interview, where Todd admits naiveté regarding Republican misinformation under the Trump administration. Rosen argues this isn't naiveté but professional malpractice, highlighting Todd's influential position and responsibility to understand political dynamics. Rosen contends Todd's failure stems from willful blindness and a lack of imagination, not a lack of knowledge.

item.title: Peabody adds six new members to board of directors
item.description: Peabody Awards has announced new members to its bicoastal board of directors. The new members, representing diverse media organizations and expertise, will provide counsel and advance Peabody's commitment to outstanding storytelling. The boards are separate from the Peabody Awards jury.

item.title: Industry leaders provide expert counsel - The Peabody Awards
item.description: Peabody Awards announced new members to its bicoastal board of directors. The new board members, representing diverse backgrounds in media and entertainment from both the East and West Coasts, will provide expert counsel and help extend Peabody's reach through new partnerships and public engagement.

item.title: Bad headline, small changes at the New York Times - PressThink
item.description: This article analyzes the internal tensions at the New York Times regarding its coverage of Donald Trump. The author, a self-described Times loyalist, highlights the growing disconnect between the paper's editorial decisions and the expectations of its core readership, particularly concerning the portrayal of Trump's racism and the handling of the 2016 election coverage. The article notes a generational divide within the Times newsroom, with younger journalists advocating for a more aggressive stance against Trump, while older journalists prefer a more traditional approach. The absence of a public editor is criticized, and the author questions the paper's ability to adapt to the changing media landscape and its evolving relationship with its audience.

item.title: Trump's attacks on journalists could incite violence, study warns
item.description: A report from the Committee to Protect Journalists warns that President Trump's attacks on the media mirror authoritarian regimes and could provoke violence against journalists. The report, titled “The Enemy Within: Trump’s War on the Press,” highlights Trump's repeated use of the term "fake news" and labeling some journalists as "enemies of the people," along with government attempts to control information access. The study suggests his rhetoric, which includes aggressive verbal assaults at rallies and on social media, endangers journalists and undermines the credibility of the U.S. press internationally. The report concludes by emphasizing the importance of defending the media from rhetoric that undermines its crucial role.

item.title: Trump attacks on journalists could be a factor in violence, study says
item.description: A study indicates that attacks on journalists in the U.S. surged in 2018, potentially linked to President Trump's repeated criticisms of the media. The report, compiled by the U.S. Press Freedom Tracker, documented a rise in physical assaults on journalists, arrests, border stops, equipment seizures, and subpoenas. The study highlights the impact of Trump's rhetoric, suggesting it contributes to an atmosphere of hostility that may sanction such attacks, making the United States a less safe place for journalists.

item.title: Creating a Space for Ad-Free Journalism with The Correspondent
item.description: This transcript discusses The Correspondent, a successful member-funded, ad-free news site from the Netherlands, and its plans to expand to English-language publishing. The discussion highlights the site's unique principles: rejecting advertising, corporate sponsors, and clickbait; focusing on in-depth reporting; and emphasizing solutions-oriented journalism. The conversation also touches upon the challenges of unbiased news coverage, particularly in the context of the Trump administration's manipulation of the press briefing room, and advocates for transparency in journalism by openly stating the journalist's perspective.

item.title: Jay Rosen pitches the English-language Correspondent on The Daily Show
item.description: The decline in trust in journalism is discussed, highlighting the closure of numerous local news outlets and the rise of alternative, less reliable information sources such as social media influencers. The article points to the role of social media in crippling journalism's business model and fostering misinformation, but also suggests that journalists share some responsibility for the current 'post-truth' environment. Jay Rosen's perspective on the issue is mentioned, emphasizing the need for further discussion, particularly given the upcoming Canadian election.

item.title: Letter to My Network: Join The Correspondent - PressThink
item.description: Jay Rosen, a prominent press critic, urges his readers to support The Correspondent, a member-funded, ad-free news site. He highlights its innovative principles, such as no ads, no clickbait, and a participatory model where members are active contributors. Rosen argues that this model offers a superior alternative to traditional journalism's reliance on advertising and its inherent biases, advocating for a more transparent, inclusive, and constructive approach to news.

item.title: Why Trump Is Winning and the Press Is Losing
item.description: This article analyzes the organized campaign to discredit the American press, spearheaded by the Republican coalition and amplified by Donald Trump. Jay Rosen details how this campaign operates on three segments of the electorate: core supporters, committed opponents, and those neither strongly supporting nor opposing Trump. The campaign's success is attributed to factors such as the rejection of independent news sources, the failure of Republican elites to push back, and the challenges posed by social media platforms. The text highlights the risks to journalism, including the erosion of trust in facts, the ineffectiveness of fact-checking, and the potential loss of institutional footing.

item.title: Journalism’s perfect storm? Confronting rising global threats from “f*ke news” to censorship, surveillance, and the killing of journalists with impunity
item.description: This panel discussion at the International Journalism Festival will address the converging threats to journalism, including the killing of journalists, imprisonment of media workers, internet shutdowns, the spread of fake news, mass surveillance, platform-driven economic challenges, declining public trust, state-sponsored harassment, and layoffs in traditional newsrooms. Experts will analyze these threats and explore collaborative solutions.

item.title: Normalizing Trump: An incredibly brief explainer - PressThink
item.description: Journalists covering Trump face a conflict: their ethical code demands reporting on his actions and words, but his incompetence, untrustworthiness, and lack of policy knowledge render much of their work absurd and painful. This leads to "normalization", where journalists downplay or reinterpret his behavior to maintain respect for the presidency and their profession.

item.title: Full transcript: New York University journalism professor Jay Rosen
item.description: Jay Rosen, a journalism professor at New York University, discussed the challenges facing professional journalists during the start of the Trump administration on an episode of Recode Media with Peter Kafka. Rosen believes the press is entering a dark and difficult period due to a confluence of factors, including President Trump's anti-press rhetoric, massive public distrust of institutions, and an organized movement, exemplified by right-wing talk radio and Breitbart, that has intentionally sought to discredit mainstream journalism to the point that their audiences believe there is no such thing as a fact-check. Rosen suggests that the press needs to move beyond traditional conventions and privileges, recommending that news organizations stop letting Trump's constant stream of tweets set the daily news agenda, adopt a "threat modeling" approach to anticipate how press freedom might erode, and learn to build trust by adopting the transparent, community-engaged methods demonstrated by reporters like David Fahrenthold.

item.title: Prospects for the American press under Trump, part two - PressThink
item.description: This article analyzes the crisis in American political journalism following the election of Donald Trump. The author argues that the existing model of political reporting is inadequate and proposes several measures to improve the situation, including uncoupling the news agenda from Trump's Twitter feed, adopting an 'outside-in' reporting pattern, increasing unpredictability in coverage, and learning from the example of David Fahrenthold's investigative reporting. The author emphasizes the need for journalists to think politically about their profession, broaden their audience engagement, and build trust with a more diverse public.

item.title: Winter is coming: prospects for the American press under Trump - PressThink
item.description: This article details a multifaceted crisis facing the American press, encompassing economic instability, declining public trust, a broken political journalism model, organized efforts to discredit mainstream media, the rise of 'verification in reverse,' and the influence of entertainment values. The author argues that these interconnected factors create a severe threat to the free press and its role as a check on power, exacerbated by Trump's presidency and the amplification of false narratives through social media. While acknowledging some positive signs, the overall tone is deeply pessimistic regarding the future of journalism.

item.title: Newspapers shouldn't apologize for telling the truth about Donald Trump
item.description: The article discusses a Florida newspaper's apology for being too critical of Donald Trump and uses this as a springboard to explore the challenges journalists face in maintaining objectivity while covering a figure who openly disregards political norms. It highlights the tension between seeking truth and avoiding criticism, arguing that the era of doing both is over, particularly when covering figures like Trump.

item.title: The Pub' #62: Jay Rosen on his love-hate relationship with public media
item.description: This article discusses a podcast episode featuring Jay Rosen, a NYU journalism professor, and his critique of public media, specifically NPR. Rosen criticizes NPR for lazy reporting and a perceived false neutrality, a concept he terms "the view from nowhere." The podcast host, Adam Ragusea, while largely agreeing with Rosen, also acknowledges the challenges faced by public media journalists and defends NPR against accusations of inherent bias, highlighting the complexities of balancing criticism and the realities of the journalistic profession. The discussion also touches upon the concentration of podcasting power in New York and the responsibility of public media to address this issue.

item.title: So I will try to explain why the Trump candidacy has been so confounding to our political press. - PressThink
item.description: This article analyzes the changing dynamics of political journalism in the context of the 2016 US presidential election, particularly the impact of Donald Trump's campaign. The author argues that the traditional 'laws of political gravity' governing campaign coverage, based on shared assumptions within the political class and media, have broken down. This breakdown is attributed to Trump's disregard for established norms and the media's struggle to adapt, leading to homogeneity in coverage and a lack of clear purpose. The author contrasts this with the approach of Jorge Ramos, who demonstrates a clear sense of purpose and audience representation, illustrating an alternative model for political journalism.

item.title: Asymmetry between the major parties fries the circuits of the mainstream press - PressThink
item.description: This article analyzes the challenges faced by mainstream political journalism during the 2016 US presidential election campaign, particularly in covering Donald Trump. The author argues that the traditional journalistic framework, based on the assumption of symmetry between the two major parties, is inadequate for understanding Trump's unconventional candidacy and the resulting asymmetric polarization. He proposes three key propositions: 1) Political journalism relies on a shared mental picture of politics that assumes similar actors with 'warring philosophies'; 2) This symmetry is disrupted by the Republican Party's extreme stance and Trump's disregard for facts and norms; and 3) The media's failure to adapt to this asymmetry resembles 'technical debt', leading to a distorted representation of reality.

item.title: Adapting Journalism to the Digital Space
item.description: NYU's Studio 20: Digital First program prepares the next generation of journalists for the digital age by focusing on practical, project-based learning in collaboration with established media companies and digital startups. The program aims to equip students with skills to innovate in digital newsrooms, bridge business, editorial, tech, and audience challenges, and regain public trust.

item.title: Verstehen, was den Journalismus derzeit verändert
item.description: Journalism is undergoing significant changes, and many struggle to understand them, often getting caught between condemning the new digital landscape or clinging to the old ways. The core issue lies in the fact that journalists are products of the changing society they are trying to understand, making it hard for them to objectively assess their own role. To better comprehend these shifts, media houses and journalists must observe society, technology, science, economics, and politics, recognizing patterns and connections rather than judging individual phenomena. Breaking down silos and fostering collaboration among various professionals is crucial to understanding and shaping the future of journalism and remaining relevant in a constantly evolving world.

item.title: Comment être au courant de ce qui change le journalisme ?
item.description: To stay informed about the evolving landscape of journalism, one should utilize various resources. Newsletters like La Matinale du Monde and Le 5 à 7 de l’AFP provide key information. Specialized websites such as Journalisme.com and Arrêt sur images offer in-depth analysis. Books like “Le Journalisme sans journalistes” and “La Fabrication de l’information” offer deeper insights. Blogs and Twitter accounts, including those of Daniel Schneidermann and Slate.fr, provide real-time updates and commentary.

item.title: The Studio 2.0 Program at NYU (directed by Jay Rosen and Clay Shirky) once again presents Open Studio Night!
item.description: Studio 2.0 at NYU, co-directed by Jay Rosen and Clay Shirky, is hosting its second Open Studio Night. The event allows the program's twelve students to showcase their projects focused on the future of news, providing opportunities for interaction, feedback, and discussion. Attendees can learn about emerging trends in journalism. The event will be held on Wednesday, November 19, 2014, at the Studio 2.0 Room in New York, NY, and requires an RSVP. Studio 2.0 emphasizes experimentation and creation, encouraging students to build prototypes and design new services in response to changes in journalism. The program prioritizes invention and creation alongside critical thinking, with a focus on practical application.

item.title: Rosen's Trust Puzzler: What Explains Falling Confidence in the Press? - PressThink
item.description: This article explores the declining public trust in news media despite improvements in journalistic professionalism. The author presents several competing explanations, including the general decline in trust across institutions, the negative influence of bad actors in media, accusations of liberal bias, strategic manipulation of journalists ('working the refs'), and a potential misalignment between journalistic professionalization and public needs. The author concludes that none of these explanations fully capture the complexity of the issue and invites further discussion.

item.title: When quoting both sides and leaving it there is the riskier call
item.description: The author critiques the 'he said, she said' approach in journalism, arguing that in situations where facts are verifiable, presenting both sides equally can be reckless and even misleading. The author uses examples from the New York Times' coverage of plagiarism accusations against a book and the BBC's handling of climate change reporting to illustrate how clinging to false equivalence can confer legitimacy on false claims and distort the truth. The author contends that the old standard of 'no position' is increasingly risky and that newsrooms need to evolve beyond this approach.

item.title: This is just a stub for a PressThink post
item.description: Jay Rosen plans to expand a post regarding The New York Times' need to explain why it published a front-page story about Russian officials releasing photos of soldiers in Ukraine that later proved false. The post initially appeared on Facebook and criticizes the newspaper's inadequate correction, specifically pointing out the lack of explanation for the new evidence and the Times' downplaying of its original assertion that Russia released the photos. The author contends that this failure hinders readers' ability to assess the images' credibility and suggests the State Department's reliance on the Times compromises the paper's value.

item.title: Pierre Omidyar plunges first $50m into media venture with Glenn Greenwald
item.description: Pierre Omidyar, founder of eBay, is investing $50 million (the first tranche of a $250 million commitment) in a new journalism venture, First Look Media, with Glenn Greenwald. This venture will consist of both a non-profit (501(c)(3)) news organization and a for-profit media technology company. The for-profit entity will support the non-profit's independent journalism. The venture's structure is compared to that of the Guardian Media Group and Bloomberg News, with Jay Rosen, a NYU professor advising the venture, highlighting its innovative funding model.

item.title: A First Look at NewCo's structure - PressThink
item.description: Pierre Omidyar's $50 million investment establishes First Look Media, a new media organization comprised of both for-profit and non-profit entities. The non-profit arm will focus on independent, public-interest journalism, while the for-profit arm will develop new media technologies. Profits from the for-profit entity will support the non-profit's journalistic mission, offering a new model for sustainable, independent journalism.

item.title: Old testament and new testament journalism - PressThink
item.description: The article contrasts two forms of journalism, "old testament" and "new testament," characterized by political argument intertwined with information and the separation of facts and values, respectively. It argues that both forms are necessary and that the rise of the internet has allowed the old testament form to gain new life, while weaknesses in new testament traditions have been exposed. The author sees a potential reconciliation and détente between the two, acknowledging the virtues and vices of each.

item.title: The NSA's next move: silencing university professors?
item.description: A Johns Hopkins professor's blog post criticizing the NSA was requested to be taken down by the university's dean, raising concerns about academic freedom. The request, seemingly originating from the university's Applied Physics Laboratory with ties to the NSA, was later retracted after media attention, highlighting the vulnerability of academic freedom to government pressure and the university's initial failure to uphold its principles.

item.title: Ungovernable reality, not Candy Crowley, threatens Obama and Romney
item.description: This article analyzes the dynamics between presidential campaigns, the Commission on Presidential Debates, and journalists moderating debates. It highlights the tension between the desire of campaigns to control the debate format and the journalist's role in pressing for answers and holding candidates accountable. The author explores different moderator styles, from the 'Vanishing Moderator' to a more active interlocutor, and argues that the lack of consensus on the ideal approach reflects a deeper question about whether presidential power needs an independent check.

item.title: Covering Wicked Problems - PressThink
item.description: The author introduces the distinction between "tame" and "wicked" problems, arguing that many issues facing society, such as climate change and failing public schools, are wicked problems—complex, ill-defined, and resistant to traditional solutions. The article proposes a new journalistic beat focused on wicked problems, suggesting that it should be a network, pattern-based, global, and reliant on diverse perspectives rather than solely on expert opinions. This beat would highlight the process of grappling with these problems, focusing on narratives of getting stuck and getting unstuck, and acknowledging the role of denial in hindering progress.

item.title: Anatomy of a Facebook Fail (mine)
item.description: The author recounts a Facebook mishap involving an event invitation. Intending to invite spouses of friends using the "suggest invitees" feature, they accidentally invited thousands of people, including all their friends and their spouses' friends. This resulted in a flood of notifications and inquiries. Due to the event's public setting, the author couldn't uninvite everyone or delete the event initially. With a friend's help, they changed the privacy settings and deleted the event. The author shares lessons learned, including the importance of caution with the "select all" feature, carefully checking privacy settings, acting quickly to address problems, seeking help when needed, and following up with those legitimately invited. The author encourages others to share their social media failures.

item.title: Adapting Journalism to the Web
item.description: Jay Rosen and Ethan Zuckerman discuss the transformation of journalism in the digital age. Rosen argues that the internet has democratized the freedom of the press, but also fragmented the mass audience. Zuckerman raises concerns about citizen journalism and the potential for misinformation, citing the Mike Daisey scandal. They explore the evolving roles of journalists, the importance of transparency, and the challenges of echo chambers. Rosen emphasizes that journalism is about relaying facts, distinguishing it from political rhetoric. Both discuss the need to support journalists in a changing media landscape and encourage greater public participation and civic dialogue.
